clinicalPearls: The commonest fish-borne, non-bacterial poisoning worldwide, acquired by eating tropical and subtropical reef fish.
Ciguatoxins originate in the dinoflagellate Gambierdiscus and bioaccumulate up the food chain, so large predatory reef fish such as barracuda, grouper, snapper and moray eel carry the highest risk.
The toxins are heat- and acid-stable, so cooking does not make the fish safe, and affected fish look, smell and taste normal.
Illness typically evolves through early gastrointestinal upset, then neurological and, in severe cases, cardiovascular features.
A characteristic symptom is altered temperature sensation, often described as cold allodynia or paradoxical temperature reversal, with dysaesthesiae of the lips and extremities.
Bradycardia and hypotension may occur in severe poisoning and warrant close cardiovascular monitoring.
Symptoms can persist for weeks to months and characteristically recur with alcohol, caffeine, exercise or further fish consumption.
Diagnosis is clinical and dietary; ciguatoxin is not detected by routine laboratory tests.
reference.pathophysiology: Ciguatoxins are lipid-soluble polyether toxins that bind a neurotoxin receptor on the voltage-gated sodium channel, shifting activation towards more negative potentials and impairing inactivation, so channels open at or near the resting membrane potential. The resulting sustained depolarisation with spontaneous, repetitive firing across sensory, motor and autonomic fibres — together with nodal and Schwann cell oedema — underlies the paraesthesiae, temperature dysperception, autonomic instability and gastrointestinal hypermotility. A related dinoflagellate toxin, maitotoxin, promotes calcium influx and may contribute to toxicity. Because the toxins are heat- and acid-stable and fat-soluble, they survive cooking and gastric acid and accumulate in fish tissue, biomagnifying in larger, older, predatory reef species that sit high in the food chain.
additionalInvestigations: Careful dietary and travel history, including the species and source of the fish
Electrocardiography and cardiac monitoring for bradyarrhythmia
Assessment of hydration status after vomiting and diarrhoea
Clinical exclusion of other seafood toxin syndromes
Specialised assay of any leftover fish for ciguatoxin where available
redFlags: Marked dehydration from vomiting and diarrhoea
reference.prognosis: Most patients recover over days to weeks, although sensory symptoms may linger for months and relapse with dietary and other triggers; fatalities are rare.
pitfalls: Mislabelling the illness as ordinary gastroenteritis and missing the neurological clues.
Confusing it with scombroid poisoning, which is histamine-mediated and responds to antihistamines.
Assuming that cooking or freezing the fish removes the risk.
Failing to counsel patients to avoid alcohol, caffeine and fish, which can precipitate relapse.
management: Provide supportive care with rehydration and correction of electrolyte disturbance following vomiting and diarrhoea
Monitor cardiovascular status and treat bradycardia and hypotension with atropine and fluids or vasopressors
Consider intravenous mannitol for acute neurological symptoms, recognising the evidence is debated and benefit greatest early
Relieve painful dysaesthesiae and cold allodynia symptomatically with agents such as gabapentinoids or amitriptyline
Advise avoidance of fish, alcohol, caffeine and nuts during recovery to prevent relapse of symptoms
Note there is no specific antitoxin, report to public health and identify the implicated fish
Involve toxicology and emergency medicine for severe or protracted cases
